commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class for all user interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
Amadeus.main() was doing three unrelated jobs: deciding what the bot
should say, deciding how it reaches the screen, and reading the user's
input. This moves the second and third into a new Ui class.

Ui now owns the Scanner, System.out, and the three presentation
constants (DIVIDER, NAME, BANNER), and exposes the vocabulary the app
actually needs: showWelcome, hasNextCommand, readCommand, showLine,
show, showError, showTask, showTaskList, showGoodbye, close.

Two details are worth noting:

- The single leading space that marks the bot's voice is now added
  inside Ui.show() rather than repeated at ~15 call sites, so no future
  message can forget it.
- showError() is currently identical to show(), but exists separately so
  error output can be styled differently later without having to work
  out which of the existing calls were errors.

This is the first step towards the Ui/Storage/Parser/TaskList split;
TaskList and the move from a static main() to an instance run() follow
in later commits.

Behaviour is unchanged: a text-UI regression run over three scenarios
(fresh start, reload of a saved file, and a deliberately corrupted save
file) produces output byte-identical to the previous commit.

Add a "find <keyword>" command that lists the tasks whose description
contains the keyword.

The matching lives in Task.descriptionContains rather than in the command
loop, mirroring how Task.occursOn already answers the "on" command. That
keeps each task responsible for answering questions about its own data and
avoids a chain of type tests at the call site.

Parser.parseKeyword takes everything after the command word as a single
keyword, so "find read book" searches for the whole phrase rather than two
separate words. A missing keyword is reported as an AmadeusException with
the correct usage, consistent with the other commands.

The match ignores case so that "find Book" also finds "read book"; a user
searching their own list should not have to remember how they capitalised
it. An empty result is reported explicitly rather than printing an empty
list, matching how "on" reports a day with nothing scheduled.

Tests cover keyword parsing (multi-word and missing) and description
matching (present, absent, and differing case).

commitResults.messageTitle: Add assert statements to document invariants
commitResults.messageBody:
Several places in the code rely on conditions that the surrounding
logic already guarantees - a parsed index staying in range, an
@FXML field being non-null after a successful load - but nothing
states that assumption anywhere; a future edit could break it
silently.

Java's assert statement exists for exactly this: a check for a
programming bug, not for bad user input (which AmadeusException
already handles), that documents the assumption and fails loudly
when enabled during development and testing.

Let's,
* assert that Parser.parseTaskIndex()'s result stays within the
  task list's bounds in the mark/unmark/delete branches of
  Amadeus.getResponse()
* assert that tasks.size() never exceeds MAX_TASKS right after a
  task is added
* assert that Storage.decodeTask() is never called with a blank
  line, since its only caller filters those out first
* assert that DialogBox's @FXML fields are non-null once the FXML
  has loaded
* assert that MainWindow.handleUserInput() never runs before
  setAmadeus() has been called
* enable assertions on the Gradle "run" task, since JavaExec
  tasks don't turn them on the way the "test" task does

Two related gaps were left unasserted, because the code does not
actually guarantee them yet: Event's "end never before start" is
never validated, and the MAX_TASKS guard uses "==" instead of ">=",
so a save file edited past 100 tasks would not trip it. Asserting
either would document a false invariant instead of a true one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Amadeus: extract each command into its own handler method
commitResults.messageBody:
getResponse() had grown into a single ~130-line method: one big
try/switch with a case per command, and the more involved commands
(on, find, mark, unmark, delete, adding a task) had their full logic
inlined right there, nested up to try -> switch -> case -> for -> if
deep. That mixes the low-level work of each command with the
high-level job of the method itself - deciding which command applies
- which the course's code quality guide calls out on two fronts: keep
methods under ~30 lines, and keep every statement in a block at the
same level of abstraction (SLAP).

Let's,
* move the body of the on/find/mark/unmark/delete/todo-deadline-event
  cases into their own private handleXxx() methods, each returning the
  reply lines for that command
* leave getResponse() as a plain dispatcher: parse the command word,
  switch on it, call the matching handler - nothing else

This is a pure extraction with no behaviour change: same inputs
produce the same replies, confirmed by the existing test suite still
passing. bye/list stay inlined since they are already one or two
statements - extracting them would add a method without removing any
complexity.

commitResults.messageTitle: Amadeus: share the filter-and-render logic in on/find
commitResults.messageBody:
handleOn() and handleFind() were separately doing the exact same
three-step dance: build a list of every task that answers some
question, then either say nothing matched or show a header followed
by the matches as a numbered list. Only the question, the header text,
and the "nothing matched" message actually differed between the two.
The course's code quality guide calls this out directly under
Minimize Code Duplication - copy-and-modified code like this should be
pulled into one shared method (the DRY principle).

Let's,
* add describeMatches(), taking the per-task question, how to word the
  header from the match count, and what to say when nothing matched
* have handleOn() and handleFind() call it instead of repeating the
  filter-then-render logic themselves

A Predicate<Task> is the natural fit for "does this task match", and
an IntFunction<String> lets the header mention how many tasks matched
without describeMatches() having to know anything about dates or
keywords - the lambda syntax already appears elsewhere in the project
(MainWindow's PauseTransition callback). Manually re-ran "on" and
"find" against the same data used before this change; the wording of
every reply is byte-for-byte the same as before, and the test suite
still passes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Amadeus: share the task lookup in mark/unmark/delete
commitResults.messageBody:
handleMark(), handleUnmark() and handleDelete() all opened with the
same line: parse the task number out of the command and look up the
task it refers to. Only what each did with that task afterwards
differed. As with the previous commit, this is exactly what the code
quality guide's Minimize Code Duplication guideline is about - the
same lookup written three times instead of once.

Let's,
* add getTaskByNumber(), which parses and validates the task number
  and returns the task at that position
* have handleMark(), handleUnmark() and handleDelete() call it instead
  of repeating Parser.parseTaskIndex() + tasks.get() themselves

handleDelete() now removes the looked-up Task object directly
(tasks.remove(Task)) instead of removing by the index it no longer
keeps around. That still removes exactly the intended task: Task does
not override equals(), so List.remove(Object) falls back to reference
equality, which can only match the one instance getTaskByNumber()
returned - confirmed by manually deleting one of two tasks with
identical descriptions and checking the other survived. Test suite
still passes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Main: name the window's minimum-size numbers
commitResults.messageBody:
start() called stage.setMinHeight(220) and stage.setMinWidth(417)
with no explanation of what those numbers are or why those particular
values were picked. The code quality guide's Avoid Magic Numbers
guideline asks for exactly this to be a named constant instead: a
reader hitting these two calls has no way to tell, at a glance, that
they're a pair defining one thing (the window's minimum size) rather
than two unrelated numbers.

Let's,
* add MIN_WINDOW_HEIGHT and MIN_WINDOW_WIDTH constants to Main, and
  use them in start() instead of the bare numbers

This only renames the two values; it does not change the window's
actual minimum size.

commitResults.messageTitle: Amadeus: use a Stream to filter tasks in on/find
commitResults.messageBody:
The "on" and "find" commands both built their match list the same
imperative way: an empty ArrayList, a for-each loop over every task,
and an if that adds the task when it passes a one-line test. That is
exactly the filter-and-collect shape the Streams API exists for, and
expressing it as a stream states the intent - keep the tasks that
pass this test - directly, instead of spelling out the accumulator
loop that produces it.

Let's,
* replace the loop in "on" with
  tasks.stream().filter(task -> task.occursOn(date)).toList()
* replace the equivalent loop in "find" with the same shape, filtering
  on task.descriptionContains(keyword) instead

toList() (rather than collect(Collectors.toList())) is enough here
since matches is only read afterwards - isEmpty(), size(), and handed
to addTaskList() - never added to or removed from, so the immutable
list it returns is not a problem.

Not every loop in the codebase was converted: Storage.load() needs
the 1-based line number for its warning messages and calls a method
that throws a checked AmadeusException, both of which fight a stream
lambda more than they simplify it, and TaskDateTime.parse() returns
from inside its loop on the first formatter that matches, which reads
more clearly as a plain loop than as a stream. Behaviour is otherwise
unchanged - confirmed by the existing tests and by manually running
"on" and "find" against both a matching and a non-matching case.
